extraction_notes.note: Six proofs have the identical body 'The proof is straightforward.', so the finishing step matches all of them to the first such environment (proof of Lemma 2.17); their proves edges were added by hand, and their positions (hence any backward flags) follow that first occurrence.
Example 4.15 repeats Example 1.14 verbatim and Example 4.13 repeats Example 3.15 verbatim; only the first copy of each is a node.

Introductory motivation was left out: Stoughton's binder rule, the categorical-combinator rule and the Abadi et al. equality (cited only to motivate), and the intro's informal restatements of the subscripted-W grammar, contexts, judgements and changed rule (vii), which Section 2 restates formally.
The label FV is defined twice (Definition 3.2 and Definition 12.1); the parser resolves \ref{FV} to Definition 3.2, which matches the intended meaning in Definition 10.12.
Convention environments (notational conventions) were typed as definition.
Section 11 is a Post canonical system given as a long list of inference rules in running text; it is extracted as one definition node.

Bold case headings '(Case W1.)' in the proof of Theorem 7.19 were treated as author labels although the parser did not list them, and in the proof of Theorem 5.1 the opening immediate sentence was prepended to the Case Beta step. The proof of Lemma 10.6 has rule-by-rule cases but almost no sentences outside displays, so it gets zero steps.
Lemmas 7.17 and 7.22 are cited from Abadi et al. and their 'proofs' are only citations, so both the lemmas and the proof nodes are marked external.
The proof of Theorem 7.20 is postponed to Section 10, where it is assembled from Theorems 10.16 and 10.27 rather than a continued proof; it is linked to them by uses edges.

nodes.statement: I chose the notation scirc M instead of [s]M, because scirclambda x.qcirclambda y.M is easy to read, this notation is close to the notation of category theory, and we can now use angle brackets to denote ordered pairs and nothing else (idcirc M looks better than langle id rangle M).\\ After some doubts I have replaced the symbol uparrow by W.

I chose the notation $s\circ M$  instead of
$[s]M$, because $s\circ\lambda x.q\circ\lambda y.M$ is easy to read,
this notation is close to the notation of category theory, and we
can now use angle brackets to denote  ordered pairs and nothing
else ($id\circ M$ looks better than $\langle id \rangle M$).\\ After some
doubts I have replaced the symbol $\uparrow$ by $\mathcal{W}$.

nodes.raw_latex:
(The calculus $\lambda\mathcal{W}$ without several rules).\\
 $
\begin{array}{lll}
(Beta) & (\lambda x.M)N\rightarrow \langle id\,,\, N\diagdown x\rangle\circ M &\\
(Abs) & s\circ \lambda x.M\rightarrow\lambda x.\langle \mathcal{W}_{x}\circ
s\,,\, x\diagdown
x\rangle\circ M &\\
(App) & s\circ (MN)\rightarrow(s\circ  M)(s\circ  N) &\\
(ConsVar) & \langle s\,,\, N\diagdown x\rangle\circ x\rightarrow N &\\
(New) & \langle s\,,\, N\diagdown x\rangle\circ y\rightarrow  s\circ y & (x\not\equiv y)\\
(IdVar) &  id\circ x\rightarrow x &\\
(Clos) & s\circ q\circ M\rightarrow (s\circ q)\circ M &\\
(Ass) & s\circ q\circ  r\rightarrow (s\circ q)\circ r &\\
(IdR) & s\circ id\rightarrow s &\\
(IdShift) & id\circ \mathcal{W}_{x}\rightarrow\mathcal{W}_{x} &\\
(ConsShift) & \langle s\,,\, N\diagdown x\rangle\circ \mathcal{W}_{x}\rightarrow s &\\
(Map) & s\circ \langle q\,,\, N\diagdown x\rangle\rightarrow\langle
s\circ q \,,\, s\circ N\diagdown x\rangle &\\
(\mathcal{W}_1) & \mathcal{W}_{x}\circ y\rightarrow y & (x\not\equiv y)\\
(\mathcal{W}_2) & (s\circ\mathcal{W}_{x})\circ y\rightarrow s\circ y & (x \not\equiv
y)\\
(\alpha_1) & \lambda x.M\rightarrow\lambda y.\langle\mathcal{W}_{y}\,,\,
y\diagdown x\rangle\circ M & (*)
\end{array}$
\\
where $(*)$ is some restriction on the variables: if the variable
$x$ occurs freely in $\lambda x.M$, we can rename $x$ to a ``good"
variable.

The sets of terms and substitutions are defined inductively as follows: M,N::&= a mid MN mid lambda a. M mid scirc M\\ s,q::&= id mid W_a mid langle s\,,\, Ndiagdown a rangle mid scirc q Note that\\[5pt] llll scirc M & corresponds to & M[s] & from ;\\ scirc q & corresponds to & qcirc s & from ;\\ langle s\,,\, Ndiagdown arangle & corresponds to & Ncdot s & from ;\\ W_a & corresponds to & uparrow & from . \\
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{pervoe} The symbols $x,y,z,\ldots$ are \emph{variables}. The symbols $M,N,L$ range over \emph{terms},
$s,q,r$  range over \emph{substitutions}, and $a,b,c$  range
over variables (they are \emph{metavariables}). The sets of terms
and substitutions are defined inductively as follows:
\begin{align*}
M,N::&= a \mid  MN \mid \lambda a. M \mid s\circ M\\
s,q::&= id \mid \mathcal{W}_{a} \mid \langle s\,,\,  N\diagdown a \rangle \mid
s\circ q
\end{align*}
Note that\\[5pt]
 $\begin{array}{llll}
 s\circ M & \text{corresponds to} & M[s] &\text{ from ~\cite{Abadi}};\\
 s\circ q & \text{corresponds to} & q\circ s &\text{ from ~\cite{Abadi}};\\
\langle s\,,\, N\diagdown a\rangle & \text{corresponds to} & N\cdot s &\text{ from ~\cite{Abadi}};\\
\mathcal{W}_{a} & \text{corresponds to} & \uparrow &\text{ from
~\cite{Abadi}}.
   \end{array}$\\

nodes.statement: The proof is by induction over the structure of s (see Definition~).\\ Case 1: s is id. This implies that Delta coincides with Gamma.\\ Case 2: s has the form W_a for some a. This implies that Gamma coincides with Delta,a.\\ Case 3: s has the form langle q\,,\, Ndiagdown arangle for some q,N,a. By Generation lemma, we can derive Gammavdash qtrianglerightSigma for some Sigma. By the induction hypothesis, Sigma is uniquely defined for Gamma and q. Then Delta coincides with Sigma,a.\\ Case 4: s has the form qcirc r for some q,r. By Generation lemma, we can derive Gammavdash qtrianglerightSigma for some Sigma. By the induction hypothesis, Sigma is uniquely defined for Gamma and q. By Generation lemma, we can derive Sigmavdash rtrianglerightDelta, where Delta is uniquely defined for Sigma and r.
nodes.raw_latex:
The proof is by induction over the structure of
$s$ (see Definition~\ref{pervoe}).\\
Case 1: $s$ is $id$. This implies that $\Delta$ coincides with
$\Gamma$.\\
Case 2: $s$ has the form $\mathcal{W}_{a}$ for some $a$. This implies
that $\Gamma$
coincides with $\Delta,a$.\\
Case 3: $s$ has the form $\langle q\,,\, N\diagdown a\rangle$ for some
$q,N,a$. By Generation lemma,  we can derive $\Gamma\vdash
q\triangleright\Sigma$ for some $\Sigma$. By the induction hypothesis,
$\Sigma$ is uniquely defined for $\Gamma$ and $q$. Then $\Delta$
coincides with
$\Sigma,a$.\\
Case 4: $s$ has the form $q\circ r$ for some $q,r$. By Generation
lemma, we can derive $\Gamma\vdash q\triangleright\Sigma$ for some $\Sigma$.
By the induction hypothesis, $\Sigma$ is uniquely defined for
$\Gamma$ and $q$. By Generation lemma, we can derive $\Sigma\vdash
r\triangleright\Delta$, where $\Delta$ is uniquely defined for $\Sigma$ and
$r$.

\\[5pt]

where the side conditions are as follows:\\[5pt]

\begin{array}{ll}

By Generation lemma, Gamma,avdash N is derivable. Suppose N contains a block of the form (W_a_1ldots a_mb)circ b. By induction hypothesis, we can apply alpha_1 or alpha_2 to Gamma,avdash N. But any application of alpha_1 or alpha_2 to Gamma,avdash N corresponds to some application of alpha_1 or alpha_2 (and, in some cases, Abs) to Gammavdashlambda a.N. For example,\\ Gamma,avdash Nrightsquigarrow_alpha_2Gamma,b vdashlangleW_b\,,\, bdiagdown aranglecirc N\\ corresponds to\\ Gammavdashlambda a.Nrightsquigarrow_alpha_1Gammavdashlambda b.langleW_b\,,\, bdiagdown aranglecirc N\\[10pt] Case 4: M has the form NL. By Generation lemma, Gammavdash N and Gammavdash L are derivable. Suppose one of these terms contains a block of the form (W_a_1ldots a_mb)circ b. For clarity, let it be N. By induction hypothesis, we can apply alpha_1 or alpha_2 to Gammavdash N. I claim that we can apply alpha_1 or alpha_2 to Gammavdash NL. For the case alpha_1 is nothing to prove, because any alpha_1-redex in N occurs in NL too. For the case alpha_2, suppose that Gammavdash NL has the form Sigma,a,Deltavdash NL. Recall that FV(NL)=FV(N)cup FV(L), hence FV(N)subseteq FV(NL). By Lemma~,\\ FV(a,Deltavdash N))subseteq FV(a,Deltavdash NL).\\ Hence if ain bigcup_igeqslant 1 FV_i(a,Deltavdash N), then ain bigcup_igeqslant 1 FV_i(a,Deltavdash NL). If we can apply alpha_2 to Sigma,a,Deltavdash N, then we can apply alpha_2 to Sigma,a,Deltavdash NL.

lemma, $\Gamma\vdash M$
has the form\\
$\Delta\,,\,b\,,\,a_m\,,\,\ldots\,,\, a_1\vdash
(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldots a_mb})\circ b$  \\
and we can apply $\alpha_2$ , because\\
 $FV(b\,,\,a_m\,,\,\ldots\,,\,
a_1\vdash (\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldots a_mb})\circ b)=\langle\{b\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle$\\[10pt]
 Case 3: $M$ has the form $\lambda a.N$. By Generation lemma, $\Gamma,a\vdash
N$ is derivable. Suppose $N$ contains a block of the form
 $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldots a_mb})\circ b$. By
induction hypothesis, we can apply $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to
$\Gamma,a\vdash N$. But any application  of $\alpha_1$ or
$\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma,a\vdash N$ corresponds to some application
of $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ (and, in some cases, $Abs$) to
$\Gamma\vdash\lambda a.N$. For example,\\
$\Gamma,a\vdash N\rightsquigarrow_{\alpha_2}\Gamma,b \vdash\langle\mathcal{W}_{b}\,,\,
b\diagdown a\rangle\circ N$\\
corresponds to\\
 $\Gamma\vdash\lambda
 a.N\rightsquigarrow_{\alpha_1}\Gamma\vdash\lambda b.\langle\mathcal{W}_{b}\,,\,
b\diagdown a\rangle\circ N$\\[10pt]
 Case 4: $M$ has the form $NL$. By Generation lemma, $\Gamma\vdash N$ and
$\Gamma\vdash L$ are derivable. Suppose one of these terms
contains a block of the form $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldots a_mb})\circ b$. For
clarity, let it be $N$. By induction hypothesis,  we can apply
$\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma\vdash N$. I claim that we can
apply $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma\vdash NL$. For the case
$\alpha_1$ is nothing to prove, because any $\alpha_1$-redex in
$N$ occurs in $NL$ too. For the case $\alpha_2$, suppose that
$\Gamma\vdash NL$ has the form $\Sigma,a,\Delta\vdash NL$. Recall
that $FV(NL)=FV(N)\cup FV(L)$, hence $FV(N)\subseteq FV(NL)$. By
Lemma~\ref{monotone},\\ $FV(a,\Delta\vdash N))\subseteq FV(a,\Delta\vdash NL)$.\\
Hence if $a\in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1} FV_i(a,\Delta\vdash N)$,
then $a\in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1} FV_i(a,\Delta\vdash NL)$. If
we can apply $\alpha_2$ to $\Sigma,a,\Delta\vdash N$, then we can
apply $\alpha_2$ to $\Sigma,a,\Delta\vdash NL$.

$\Gamma\vdash M$ is derivable by
Lemma~\ref{poleznaya}. $\Sigma\vdash L$ is derivable by Subject
reduction. Therefore $L$ is pure  and $V$ is a $\sigma$-normal
form (Theorem~\ref{pure}, Lemma~\ref{purelemma}). Why
$U\overset{\sigma}{\rightarrow\rightarrow}V$? It is sufficient to prove that
$\sigma(U)\equiv\sigma(V)$ ($U$ reduces to its $\sigma$-normal
form because $\sigma$ is strongly normalizing and confluent). The
proof is by induction over the length of the reduction sequence $
\Gamma\vdash M\overset{\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha}{\rightsquigarrow\rightsquigarrow}\Sigma\vdash L$. If
this length is equal to $0$, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise,
suppose this sequence has the form
\\
$\Gamma\vdash M\rightsquigarrow\ldots\rightsquigarrow\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow\Sigma\vdash L$,\\
where
 $(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}W$ and $\sigma(U)\equiv\sigma(W)$.\\
   Any possible $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-reduction  step $\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow\Sigma\vdash L$,
except  $New,\mathcal{W}_1,\mathcal{W}_2,\alpha_1$, and $\alpha_2$ corresponds to
the same name $\sigma$-reduction step of the  nameless terms
$W\rightarrow V$, hence $\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$ in these cases. For
$\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ use Lemma~\ref{lemmauparrow}.\\

\qquad(a\neq b)$

 b}}{\Gamma,a\vdash\mathcal{W}_{a}\circ b}\qquad

 $(\Gamma\vdash b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n}$;\\
  then\\
$(\Gamma,a\vdash\mathcal{W}_{a}\circ
b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\mathcal{W}\circ\underline{n}$ and\\
$(\Gamma,a\vdash b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n+1}$.\\
We see that
$\sigma(\mathcal{W}\circ\underline{n})\equiv\sigma(\underline{n+1})$.
\\[5pt]

b\rightarrow s\circ b \qquad(a\neq b)$

u$;\\
 $(\Gamma\vdash
 b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n}$;\\
then\\

$(\Gamma,a\vdash b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} \underline{n+1}$;\\
$(\Delta\vdash s\circ b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}
u\circ\underline{n+1}$.\\
We see that\\
$\sigma((u\circ\mathcal{W})\circ\underline{n})\equiv\sigma(u\circ\underline{n+1})$\\[5pt]
(\textbf{Case} ${\mathbf{New}}.) \quad \langle s\,,\, N\diagdown a\rangle\circ
b\rightarrow s\circ b \qquad(a\neq b)$
$$\ruletwo{\ruletwo{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash
s\triangleright\Gamma}}{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash N}}{\Delta\vdash\langle s\,,\, N\diagdown
a\rangle\triangleright\Gamma,a}}{\ruleone{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash
 b}}{\Gamma,a\vdash b}}{\Delta\vdash\langle s\,,\, N\diagdown a\rangle\circ
b}\qquad \ruletwo{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash
s\triangleright\Gamma}}{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash b}}{\Delta\vdash s\circ b}$$
Suppose \\
$(\Delta\vdash s\triangleright\Gamma)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}
u$;\\
$(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} V$;\\
$(\Gamma\vdash b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n}$;\\
then\\
$(\Gamma,a\vdash b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n+1}$;\\
$(\Delta\vdash\langle s\,,\, N\diagdown a\rangle\circ
b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\langle
u\,,\, V\rangle\circ\underline{n+1}$;\\
$(\Delta\vdash s\circ b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}
u\circ\underline{n}$.\\
We see that\\
$\sigma(\langle u\,,\, V\rangle\circ\underline{n+1})\equiv\sigma(\langle u\,,\,
V\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}\circ\underline{n})\equiv\sigma(u\circ\underline{n})$.

The proof is by induction over the length of the reduction sequence $\Gamma\vdash M\overset{\lambda\mathcal{W}}{\rightsquigarrow\rightsquigarrow}\Sigma\vdash
L$.  If this length is equal to $0$, there is nothing to prove.
Otherwise, suppose this sequence has the form
\\
$\Gamma\vdash M\rightsquigarrow\ldots\rightsquigarrow\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow\Sigma\vdash L$,\\
where
$(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}  W$ and  $\sigma(U)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\rightarrow\rightarrow}\sigma(W)$.\\
If the reduction step $\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow\Sigma\vdash L$ belongs to
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$, everything is all right, because
$\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$ in this case. Indeed, $\Gamma\vdash M$
is derivable by Lemma~\ref{poleznaya}. $\Delta\vdash N$ and
$\Sigma\vdash L$ are derivable by Subject
reduction. Take any $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form of $\Sigma\vdash L$ (this normal form exists by Theorem ~\ref{SN} and are derivable too) and use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem} to get $ W\overset{\sigma}{\rightarrow\rightarrow}\sigma(V)$.\\

$W\rightarrow_{Beta}V$, because any $Beta$-redex in $N$ corresponds to
some $Beta$-redex in $W$, hence
$\sigma(W)\rightarrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ by Lemma~\ref{lemmapodjom}.

\end{align*}

nodes.raw_latex:
Suppose we have some infinite $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$ M_1\rightarrow M_2\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow M_n\rightarrow\ldots$$
 I claim that we can get
some
infinite  $R$-sequence\\
$$(M_1)^*\overset{R}{\rightarrow\rightarrow}(M_2)^*\overset{R}{\rightarrow\rightarrow}\ldots\overset{R}{\rightarrow\rightarrow}(M_n)^*\overset{R}{\rightarrow\rightarrow}\ldots$$
The proof is by induction over $n$. If $n$ is equal to $1$, there is nothing to prove. Else there are three cases.\\[5pt]
1)  If the reduction step $ M_n\rightarrow M_{n+1}$ is not
$Abs,\alpha_1,\alpha_2$, we can apply the\\ $R$-reduction of the
same name $(M_n)^*\rightarrow( M_{n+1})^*$, but then might need several
$\xi$-steps, because $ConsVar, New, ConsShift,\mathcal{W}_1,\mathcal{W}_2$ can
decrease $FV$. If any of these reductions is applied under some
black lambda, this lambda may
turn pale. See Example~\ref{example1.18}.\\[5pt]
2) If  $M_n\rightarrow_{\alpha_1} M_{n+1}$,
we can apply $\alpha$:\\
$(M_n)^*\rightarrow_{\alpha}(M_{n+1})^*$ (see Lemma~\ref{restriction}
and
Example~\ref{example1.13}).\\[5pt]
3) If $ M_n\rightarrow_{Abs} M_{n+1}$ and the $Abs$-redex is
$s\circ\lambda a.M$, there are four
possible subcases:\\
$
\begin{array}{lll}
Subcase \,1. & a\notin FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\notin
FV_1(\lambda
 a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a\diagdown a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase\, 2. & a\in FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\in FV_1(\lambda
 a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a\diagdown a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase\, 3. & a\notin FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\in FV_1(\lambda
 a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a\diagdown a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase \,4. & a\in FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\notin FV_1(\lambda
 a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a\diagdown a\rangle\circ M);
\end{array}\\[3pt]
$ and we can apply $Abs_1, Abs_2, Abs_3$, and $Abs_4$,
respectively. See Examples~\ref{example1.14}, \ref{example1.15},
\ref{example1.16}, and \ref{example1.17}.

The proof is similar for substitutions. For judgements, suppose we
have some infinite $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$\Gamma_1\vdash M_1\rightsquigarrow\Gamma_2\vdash  M_2\rightsquigarrow\Gamma_3\vdash M_3\rightsquigarrow\ldots$$
We can obtain the $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence of terms
$$\Lambda\Gamma_1.M_1\rightarrow\rightarrow\Lambda\Gamma_2.M_2\rightarrow\rightarrow\Lambda\Gamma_3.M_3\rightarrow\rightarrow\ldots$$
where $\alpha_2$-steps are replaced by $\alpha_1$ and $Abs$.
